PREFACE 

For some time there has been a demand from the profession for a revised and more adequate book of forms. Furthermore, a desire has been expressed for such a book to contain not only numerous additional forms, but also reasonably complete annotations to not only the case law relating thereto, but to the various statutes involved, which are sometimes easily overlooked.

Since the original publication of Searl's Forms, there have been numerous changes in the court rules (notably in the 1938 revision). 

This, along with certain statutory changes in individual proceedings, also made it desirable to revise the original volume. 

In preparing this work, the author has endeavored to annotate the forms with particular reference to the statutes and court rules involved, and to include substantive law only in so far as it appeared requisite to intelligent use and understanding of the forms and proceedings. The author, however, makes no pretense of exhaustive annotation on the subject, the attempt having been rather to indicate all matters of law and procedure to which it seemed necessary to call attention, although a reasonably complete annotation of certain less familiar questions has at times been indulged in. 

The author has included a large number of specific declarations and bills of complaint which did not appear in the original volume, and has also included forms for answers both at law and equity, particularly including various forms involving affirmative defenses and answers to declarations relating to insurance. Also, numerous forms for orders and judgments, such as the various judgments in replevin, have been included, and the same has been done for returns and other routine matters. A new treatment of intervention and declaratory judgments has been added and also the matter of the enforcement of judgments and decrees, forms for capias ad satisfaciendum, for proceedings at law in the nature of judgment creditor's bills, for body execution in chancery, for the sale of real estate under decree, for writs of assistance, for contempt proceedings and ne exeat. Forms for circuit court commissioner's proceedings relating to foreclosure, summary proceedings for the recovery of land, and proceedings in the new court of claims, have been included. 

Likewise, the appellate forms are largely new, the proceedings in supreme court appeals having been revised in accordance with the new rules, and forms relating to appeals in Wayne County from the probate court, circuit court commissioner, common pleas court, municipal courts, justice's courts, etc., having been included. A new seciii

PREFACE 

tion treating appeals from the Michigan Unemployment Compensation Commission has also been added. The foregoing, while not a list of the changes which have been made, is indicative of the scope of the work. 

An attempt has been made to conform to the author's idea of a properly modernized pleading and practice by the elimination of much archaic phraseology and surplusage. It is the hope of the author that this simplification will be found to be an improvement over the older forms, and that the work is sufficiently complete to furnish a form or at least a helpful pattern or suggestion for a form to fit almost any need. 

This revised portion of Judge Searl's work is now to be published in two volumes, instead of one, as formerly, by reason of its greatly increased size. Distribution of the material between two volumes will permit continuation of ready pocket supplementation over a long period of time, in the absence of radical changes in the practice. 

The contents of these two volumes are separately indexed in a special index to forms in the back of Volume 4A, which, it is believed, the user will find of considerable convenience in quickly locating the particular form desired. 

The author desires to acknowledge the invaluable assistance in the preparation of this work of his son and law partner, Charles F. 

Cummins, and of Elijah G. Poxson, Jr., associated with him in the practice of law. 

Lansing, Michigan 

July 12, 1940

ALVA M. CUMMINS

NOTE. C. L. 1929, § 4790, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 9.1701, provides for service upon the secretary of state or his deputy in civil actions against nonresident operators or nonresident owners of motor vehicles operated on Michigan highways, under certain conditions. Under such procedure, however, the statute requires that fol- 13

No. 20

summons shall 66 # #99 66 # lowing service upon the official, notice of such service together with a copy of the forthwith be + * either served upon the defendant by the sheriff or constable in the county in which he resides or sent by registered mail by the plaintiff or his attorney to the defendant * # The affidavit here set forth is designed to satisfy the requirements for proof of service as required by a proviso in the statute above quoted after notice of service and copy of summons have been sent defendant by registered mail. 

Note that the statute above quoted does not require that duplicate copies of the summons be served, nor does it provide that the copy of the summons may be left with the person in charge of the office if the secretary of state and his deputy are both absent, as is provided in C. L. 1929, § 14097, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 27.764. Careful practice would seem to require a reconcilement of these two statutes.

 in an action against a partnership one seeks more than a mere judgment against two or more individuals. The recovery is sought against them in their peculiar legal relationship as co-partners, with the rights and liabilities incident thereto. Attachment prior to the maturity of the debt is an extraordinary remedy, and the reasons assigned for issuance of the writ must be alleged in the affidavit with particularity. Thus, in 

Howell v. Muskegon Circuit Judge, 88 

Mich. 361, 367, 50 N. W. 306, it was said, in denying the writ: "The affidavit would have been sufficient to obtain a writ of attachment if the debt had been due; but, in order to avail himself of the most extraordinary remedy given by this statute, the reason for its issue must be shown by facts 

Circuit Judge.57 and circumstances so given in detail that the circuit judge can satisfy himself from such facts and circumstances that the writ ought to issue. It will not do for the affiant simply to swear that he knows that the defendant in the suit has assigned, disposed of, or concealed his property with intent to defraud his creditors. The facts attending such disposition or concealment of the property must be set forth, and its relation as to value to the remainder of the property owned by the debtor, so that the court may know something about it as well as the affiant."' 

57 The order for issuance of the writ must be indorsed upon the affidavit, and it is insufficient if it is indorsed upon the writ itself. Howell v. Muskegon 

Circuit Judge, 88 Mich. 369, 50 N. W. 308.

NOTE. Filing statutory notice would seem, from the wording of the statute, to be a condition precedent to a lien attaching. The statute reads: "Real estate attached shall be bound, and the attachment shall be a lien thereon from the time when a certified copy of the attachment, with a description of the real estate attached, shall be deposited in the office of the register of deeds in the county where the real estate attached is situated." C. L. 1929, § 14774, Mich. 

Stat. Ann. § 27.1772. In spite of this provision, however, the Michigan court has held that an unrecorded prior mortgage has priority over a subsequent attachment, although the attaching creditor had no notice of the mortgage at the time he brought the proceeding. Campbell v. Keys, 30 Mich. 127, 89 N. W. 720. Also see First Nat. Bank of Durand v. Phillpotts, 155 Mich. 331, 336, 119 N. W. 1, where the priority of attachment liens is distinguished from priority given execution liens.

§ 27.1780. 

Publication under this section is a substitute for personal service, and is necessary to enable the court to obtain jurisdiction. 

Thompson v. Thomas, 11 Mich. 274. 

King v. Harrington, 14 Mich. 532. 

And a failure to strictly comply with the statute will invalidate a subsequent judgment. Thus, in King v. Harrington, supra, where a return of no service on defendant was premature, a judgment based upon a subsequent publication was a nullity. In Wells v. Walsh, 25 Mich. 344, a judgment entered prior to proof of publication was said to be "irregular and erroneous, " and in Millar v. Babcock, 29 Mich. 526, where plaintiff failed to publish the notice within thirty days after the return day of the writ, as required by the statute, it was held that the court lost jurisdiction.

But where an attachment is brought against two joint debtors, their joint property is seized and personal service is had upon one, it is not necessary, under the act, to publish against the other. 

Hubbardston Lumber Co. v. Covert, 35 Mich. 254. 

Smith v. Runnells, 94 Mich. 617, 620, 54 N. W. 375.

It is, of course, a general rule that any form of substituted service must conform strictly to the statute. Thompson v. Thomas, 11 Mich. 274; King v. 

Harrington, 14 Mich. 532; Millar v. 

Babcock, 29 Mich. 526; Johnson v. Delbridge, 35 Mich. 436; Woolkins v. Haid, 49 Mich. 299, 13 N. W. 598; Rolfe v. 

Dudley, 58 Mich. 208, 24 N. W. 657.

And there is no exception to the rule here. Estlow v. Hanna, 75 Mich. 219, 42 N. W. 812; Jaffray v. Jennings, 101 

Mich. 515, 60 N. W. 52. See Schoenfeld v. Bourne, 159 Mich. 139, 123 

N. W. 537, wherein the notice describing one of the defendants, designating him as "William H. Dunton,'' rather than "" 'William H. Denton, "" was held to be fatally defective on a motion to quash, despite the rule of idem sonans. 54

NOTE. A petition for dissolution is a part of a statutory proceeding, and the statute must be strictly followed. See text, Vol. 2, § 578, and footnote 98. Also the statute, C. L. 1929, § 14810, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 27.1808. On the hearing of the petition, C. L. 1929, § 14812, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 27.1810, provides that if the judge or commissioner "be satisfied that such plaintiff had not a good and legal cause for suing out such writ" the attachment shall be dissolved. The Michigan cases hold that the determination must be made on the facts as they appear at the time of the hearing. No matter how well founded the basis for plaintiff's belief, if, in fact, no ground existed authorizing the issuance of the writ, dissolution must be given. Folsom v. Teichner, 27 Mich. 107. Since a petition for dissolution is a wholly statutory procedure, it is not available to attack other defects than that the plaintiff has not a "good and legal cause for suing out such writ." The inquiry is only concerned with truth of the grounds set forth in the affidavit. Vinton v. Mead, 17 Mich. 388. Conversely, the only mode by which the basis for the affidavit can be questioned is by petition for dissolution. 

The question is not properly raised by plea in abatement. Bower v. Town, 12 

Mich. 230. A third party "whose property may be attached by virtue of such writ" may also petition for such dissolution, but only on the foregoing grounds.

NOTE. The remedy of garnishment is in derogation of the common law, and the statute is strictly construed. The affidavit in garnishment is the basis of the jurisdiction, and a strict compliance with the statute is essential. Chapman v. Detroit Metropolitan Corp., 268 Mich. 391, 394, 256 N. W. 459; Pere Marquette 

Ry. Co. v. Western Heater Dispatch, 284 Fed. 574. The affidavit, above all, must conform to the statute. Thus, in Gold v. Weisman, 279 Mich. 352, 354, 272

N. W. 703, it was held: "While strict observance of statutory requirements is essential, after a proper affidavit has been filed, a substantial compliance is sufficient in the absence of fraud or mistake or any showing that one has been misled through a slight error. * * *"" And this deponent further says that he is justly apprehensive of the loss of said sum of tiff from the said dollars, so due to the said plainthe above named defendant, unless a writ of garnishment issue to the said 77 It is jurisdictionally essential that the exact amount due be stated in the affidavit. In Chapman v. Detroit Metropolitan Corp., 268 Mich. 391, 256 N. W. 

459, the affidavit averred that principal defendant was indebted to plaintiff in sums not exceeding certain amounts. 

In dismissing the writ the court said: "It is manifest that the affidavits did not state given amounts but only much or little within stated sums.

The affidavit is the foundation upon which arises jurisdiction to issue the writ of garnishment, and the statute requires that the exact amount claimed be given. Given amounts were not stated in the affidavits for the writs and the court acquired no jurisdiction.” 

78 It is proper to include in a single affidavit allegations that the garnishee defendant has property etc. in his custody and control and also that he is indebted to defendant. In Peninsular 

Stove Co. v. Circuit Judge of Wayne 

County, 85 Mich. 400, 48 N. W. 549, it was said, at p. 406: "It may often happen that the person garnished may be indebted to the principal defendant, and have property in his possession or under his control belonging to the principal defendant. In all such cases the statute does not require that the proceedings shall be separate, requiring separate suits and separate affidavits to reach the property and the indebtedness. It would be an unnecessary multiplication of suits, and we do not see that any good purposes could be accomplished by such separate proceedings. * 27

Now comes the said garnishee, and, for disclosure touching his liability as garnishee of the said § 14858, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 27.1856.

The question of whether the garnishee defendant is liable, however, depends upon the state and nature of the claim as of this time. Old Second Nat. Bank of Bay City v. Williams, 112 Mich. 564, 71 N. W. 150. Thus, the liability of an insurer to creditors of insured must be determined as of the time of service of process. Isaac Van Dyke Co. v. Moll, 241 Mich. 255, 217 N. W. 29. Strict application of the foregoing two rules would seem to be modified somewhat by the decisions. Thus, in Erb-Kidder Co. v. Levy, 262 Mich. 62, 247 N. W. 107, it was held that while the statute permits garnishment of "any debts due or to become due,' "' writs issued to reach monthly instalments of rent payable in advance were premature and wholly abortive when sued out before the instalments became due, and in 

Cogswell v. Mitts, 90 Mich. 353, 51 

N. W. 514, it was said, at page 355: "It has been repeatedly ruled that a garnishee process cannot reach an indebtedness created after the issue of the writ."' It will be noted here that in these cases the court is looking to the date of issuance rather than the time of service in determining liability, and hence it would also seem necessary to find affirmatively, as an additional factor, whether the liability was in existence at the time the writ was issued. principal defend Plaintiff's affidavit for a writ of garnishment is, in legal effect, a declaration against the garnishee defendant, and the disclosure operates as an answer thereto. C. L. 1929, § 14867, Mich.

Stat. Ann. § 27.1865. Admissions in the disclosure have the same legal effect as admissions in an answer. They need not be proved, and are prima facie evidence of the admitted matters. Allen 

V. Hazen, 26 Mich. 142.

While disclosure as made is binding and conclusive on the garnishee defendant, garnishee cannot by his disclosure prejudice the rights of third parties, Shank v. Lippman, 249 Mich. 22, 227 

N. W. 710, or the rights of principal defendant, People's Wayne County 

Bank v. Stott, 246 Mich. 540, 224 N. W. 

352, or of plaintiff, Fearey v. Cummings, 41 Mich. 376, 1 N. W. 946. 

Amendment of a disclosure rests within the discretion of the trial court. 

Dunn v. Detroit Sav. Bank, 118 Mich. 

547, 77 N. W. 6. 

Hayes v. Ross, 236 Mich. 208, 210 

N. W. 292. 

Further or supplemental disclosure may also be made. 

Butler v. Wendell, 57 Mich. 62, 23 

N. W. 460. 

Drake v. Lake Shore & M. S. Ry. Co., 69 Mich. 168, 37 N. W. 70.

Allen v. Hamburg-Bremen Fire Ins. 

Co., 121 Mich. 86, 79 N. W. 915. 74

Under these sections no allegation that the chattels, etc., are the property of plaintiff is necessary but merely the allegation "that the defendant received the property to be delivered to plaintiff when thereunto afterwards re- quested." Business Address. 

NOTE. Rule 19, § 1, Michigan Court Rules, provides: "Sec. 1. The declara tion shall contain such specific allegations as will reasonably inform the defendant of the nature of the cause he is called upon to defend. Each allegation shall be set forth in a separate paragraph, and the various paragraphs shall be numbered consecutively.' 

Clearly the statutory form does not conform to this requirement but is analogous to the form of the common counts. See O'Rourke v. Deffenbaugh, 280 Mich. 407, 273 N. W. 749; Michigan Aero Club v. Shelley, 283 Mich. 401, 278 N. W. 121; etc. However, see Von Zellen v. Westrom, 274 Mich. 555, 265

N. W. 463, which seems to indicate that the court might be disposed to uphold such a declaration in the absence of a motion to dismiss under which permission to amend would be granted.

NOTE. It would seem necessary to set up any lien, special property, or part ownership in the answer. C. L. 1929, § 14839, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 27.1837, permitted this proof to be introduced without such pleading; however, proof of such interest unless it is one conferring the right of possession does not, strictly speaking, controvert plaintiff's allegation of ownership nor does it controvert the allegation of unlawful detention on the part of defendant; where it is a possessory right it of course does controvert those allegations, but even then it establishes an affirmative right in the defendant; therefore, it seems to come clearly within that class of proof required to be set up in the answer under Rule 23, §§ 1, 2, Michigan Court Rules. These rules supersede the statute. Shrager v. Rich, 242 Mich. 419, 218 N. W. 675, etc. See Searl's Michigan Court Rules, Rule 1, note.

No. 200

No. 198. Instruction as to boundaries. 

It is the law, gentlemen, that purchasers of town lots have a right to locate them according to the stakes which they find planted and recognized, and no subsequent survey can be allowed to unsettle their lines, and the question afterwards is not whether the stakes were where they should have been in order to make them correspond with the lot lines as they should be if the platting was done with absolute accuracy, but it is whether they were planted by authority and the lots were purchased and taken possession of in reliance upon them. If such was the case, they must govern, notwithstanding any errors in locating the stakes,90

95 The assignee sues in his own name under the Real Party in Interest statute, C. L. 1929, § 14010, Mich. Stat. 

Ann. § 27.654. The test is: Would a satisfaction of judgment by plaintiff discharge the debtor? Sharrar V. 

Wayne Sav. Ass'n, 254 Mich. 456, 236 

N. W. 833; Johnson v. National Fire 

Ins. Co., 254 Mich. 126, 235 N. W. 864. 

Also see text, Vol. 1, § 20 et seq. 

The use of the word "assignee" after the plaintiff's name has been held not to state or infer that the cause of action was assigned subsequent to accrual, but was held to be merely descriptio personae. Bloom v. Sexton, 

33 Mich. 181.

It has been held that an allegation setting forth the assignment to plaintiff is unnecessary and improper in actions of replevin and trover, since it is merely a matter of evidence. Warren v. Dwyer, 91 Mich. 414, 417, 51 N. W. 1062.

However, in other assignable tort actions, in real actions, and actions on contract, the failure to allege the assignment may be fatal. 

Blackwood v. Brown, 32 Mich. 104. 

Rose v. Jackson, 40 Mich. 29. 

Altman v. Fowler, 70 Mich. 57, 37 

N. W. 708. ? his attorney, (Or, if by sum- 

Gates v. Comstock, 107 Mich. 546, 65 N. W. 544. 

McKnight v. Lowitz, 176 Mich. 452, 142 N. W. 769. 

And when an action is brought on the common counts, recovery may not be had unless the assignment is alleged. Pierce v. Closterhouse, 96 Mich. 

124, 127, 55 N. W. 663; Conrad Seipp 

Brewing Co. v. McKittrick, 86 Mich. 

191, 48 N. W. 1086, wherein plaintiff could not recover on the common counts because a note sued on, and attached to the declaration, was held to be nonnegotiable, and hence the endorsement on the back thereof was insufficient to show an assignment in the absence of an affirmative allegation in the declaration.

But where a bill of particulars given in an action on the common counts sets forth the assignment, the requirement that the assignment be set forth in the declaration is eliminated. Snell V. 

Gregory, 37 Mich. 500. Similarly in an action on an open account where copies of the account and assignment are served on defendant together with a declaration on the common counts. 

Morrill v. Bissell, 99 Mich. 409, 58 

N. W. 324. 142

No. 237. Action on open account. 

1. That between 

19-, and 19-, plaintiff sold and delivered to defendant, at his request, certain goods on open account, of which a copy is hereto attached marked exhibit A. 

2. That in consideration thereof defendant promised to pay for the same when requested.15 

3. That, although demand has been made on defendant,16 no part of said account has been paid (except the sums credited as shown by said copy of said account) and the entire balance thereof is now due. and unpaid.17

NOTE. The pleader should note the distinction between a mere open account and a mutual and open account current. In the former, the statute of limitations will bar items more than six years old, in the latter the statute runs from the last item proved in the account. C. L. 1929, § 13977, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 27.606.

For the distinction between a mere open account and a mutual account, see: 

Kimball v. Kimball, 16 Mich. 211; Hillebrands v. Nibbelink, 40 Mich. 646, wherein the failure to set up a claim as part of a mutual account brought it within the statute; In re Estate of Hiscock, 79 Mich. 536, 44 N. W. 947; Bay 

City Iron Co. v. Emery, 128 Mich. 506, 87 N. W. 652; Goodsole v. Jeffery, 202 

Mich. 201, 168 N. W. 461; Fuerbringer v. Herman, 225 Mich. 76, 195 N. W. 693; 

Lannen v. Teller, 228 Mich. 243, 200 N. W. 166. Also see text, Vol. 1, § 445, and notes in 1 A. L. R. 1060; 39 A. L. R. 369; 57 A. L. R. 201.

While convenient, this form should be used with discrimination. In actuality, it is an abbreviated use of the common counts in indebitatus assumpsit, adopted from the early practice in the Eastern States. See Page v. Babbit, 21 N. H. 389, 390, wherein the practice is referred to as recognized in 1791. In certain code states, statutes provide specifically that the pleader may use a single "count on an account annexed" when one or more items are claimed, any of which 15 It would seem prudent to allege a promise to pay. See note 22, infra. 

16 It would seem best to allege a demand, although such an allegation has been held unnecessary where an action is brought for the price of goods sold and delivered where the contract itself does not impose that condition. 1 C. J. 

651, § 153 and cases therein cited. 

17 The exception as to sums credited is inserted because, although this form is intended for use where there is no mutuality of accounts, it is theoretically possible to have a mere open account wholly lacking in mutuality with sums credited by one party to the other. See 

Kimball v. Kimball, 16 Mich. 211; 

In re Estate of Hiscock, 79 Mich. 536; 

Goodsole v. Jeffery, 202 Mich. 201, 168 

N. W. 461. 156

L. 1929, § 14206, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 27.901 and Court Rule No. 17, § 5, which makes a document attached to a pleading part of the pleading.

No. 253

Pack, 6 Mich. 240; but where the action is also against an indorser thereof a declaration which fails to allege either presentment and notice or waiver thereof is insufficient. Barber v. Taylor, 1 Mich. 352. Also see on the substantive law: 

Sieder v. Jerome, 258 Mich. 249, 241 N. W. 834; United States Radiator Corp. v. Canvasser, 259 Mich. 540, 244 N. W. 156; Robb v. Ranney, 264 Mich. 144, 249

N. W. 464. And for a case holding that the facts did not constitute waiver, Jassy v. Marciniak, 260 Mich. 153, 244 N. W. 432. Waiver will not be implied from doubtful acts. Kramer v. Stryker, 274 Mich. 179, 264 N. W. 618. The endorsement of a new note to take up an old does constitute waiver however. 

Genesee County Sav. Bank v. Rosenthal, 265 Mich. 291, 251 N. W. 334.

Also for a discussion of the law that a waiver etc., on the face of the instrument binds all endorsers but that waivers not appearing on the face of the note must appear in conjunction with the indorser's signature in such a manner as to indicate an adoption thereof by him, see, People's Nat. Bank of Ypsilanti v. 

Dicks, 258 Mich. 441, 242 N. W. 825.

51 Consult text, Vol. II, Chap. XLIX 

(p. 233). By statute, the action of trover is abolished and an action of trespass on the case for conversion substituted. C. L. 1929, § 14007, Mich. 

Stat. Ann. § 27.651, and by the same statute the tort may be waived and suit brought in assumpsit where the property is converted into money. At common law the conversion had to arise from a contract and be the conversion of personal property into money or its equivalent.

The owner cannot waive the tort and sue in assumpsit for the value of machinery sold to defendant by plaintiff's agent as his own property where defendant is still in possession of the machinery. McCormick Harvesting 

Mach. Co. v. Waldo, 128 Mich. 135, 87 N. W. 55. 

Also an action to pay over money must be in assumpsit and not in tort for conversion unless there is an obligation to pay over specific money in which case action may be brought for conversion. Thrift v. Haner, 286 Mich. 495, 282 N. W. 219, and cases cited therein. 

See article, "Qualifying as Plaintiff in Conversion," by Edward H. Warren, 49 Harv. L. Rev. 1084. Prof. Warren says: "Trover has had its long day, and the usual situation now is that a plaintiff brings, not an action of trover, but an action of tort for a conversion.

This is important. Modern courts are not necessarily bound by the trover precedents. But the old law as to trover is the background, a very useful and important background, for the law of conversion."'

With regard to whether an owner who has leased to another may be held liable as to the demised premises, see the recent case of Potter v. New York, O. & W. Ry. Co., 261 N. Y. 489, 185 

N. E. 708, where it was held that a railroad company which owned a coal trestle but let pocket therein to a coal company for the latter's exclusive use, as a matter of law was not liable for death of latter's employee resulting when ladder in pocket broke from its fastenings.

The evidence disclosed that the coal company had obtained permission from the railroad to occupy coal pockets at stated rental, and that it occupied coal pocket in question exclusively and stored coal therein. The coal company's employees entered the pocket through a trapdoor in deck trestle and did work therein, and railroad employees apparently never entered pocket except on rare occasions to make needed repairs.

Thus the railroad company, having 225

No. 310

not in any way the result of contributory negligence on the part of plaintiff.") 62 parted with possession, lost power to exclude or to invite. 

The court said: "Liability for injuries or death, suffered by a visitor to dangerous structures or premises arises from occupancy, not from ownership. The occupant having exclusive possession may forbid entrance to all visitors, in which case, with some exceptions, no duty of care arises, and the visitor may not complain if injured.

On the other hand, the occupant having such possession alone may give an invitation, or grant permission to make entry. In that case a duty of care does arise to bind the occupant, the nature and extent of which depends upon the character of the visitor, as determined by the invitation or permission extended. Thus the duty of active care to make the premises safe is owed to an invitee, or business visitor; whereas, the duty of disclosing or eliminating a known danger is the measure of the duty owed to a gratuitous licensee. As no duty whatever arises except through invitation or permission, and the measure of that duty depends upon whether there has been given the one or the other, ordinarily the duty of care, if any, binds no other than the occupant, who alone has power to invite or license. This may be subject to some exceptions, such as when the owner leases dangerous premises knowing that the tenant will invite the public to visit the same. However, generally speaking, the owner, having parted with possession, and lost power to exclude or to invite, cannot be liable if the visitor be injured. These principles are universally acknowledged to be the law upon the subject. Salmond on the Law of Torts, p. 452; The Law of Torts, Pollock (13th Ed.), p. 527; Shearman & Redfield on the Law of Negligence, 

§ 704; Restatement of the Law of 

Torts, §§ 212, 213, 227; Haefeli v. 

Woodrich Engineering Co., 255 N. Y. 

442, 175 N. E. 123; Cullings v. Goetz, 256 N. Y. 287, 176 N. E. 397. 'The person responsible for the condition of the premises is he who is in possession of them for the time being, whether he is the owner or not. For it is he who has the immediate supervision and control and the power of permitting or prohibiting the entry of other persons.' 

Salmond, supra, 445, 446. The power of control, necessary to raise the duty of care, 'implies the power and the right to admit people to the premises and to exclude people from them.' 

Cavalier v. Pope, [1906] App. Cas. 428, 433. In the case of a tenant's possession under a lease, the landlord is not liable, even though he assumes the duty to repair the premises. Cullings v. 

Goetz, supra. In that case Chief Judge

Cardozo stated: 'Liability in tort is an incident to occupation or control.' 

Page 290 of 256 N. Y., 176 N. E. 397, 398,"

(2d) 949, Judge Phillips said: "While there is no implied warranty by the landlord that the leased premises are safe or fit for occupancy, the landlord is liable for injuries resulting to the tenant from latent defects in the premises known to the landlord and concealed from the tenant."'

If plaintiff elects the first course and rescinds he must of course first tender back the property (except in equity) and then sue for the recovery of the price paid. Barnhardt v. Hamel, 207

Mich. 622, 170 N. W. 72; Davidter v. 

Ash, 264 Mich. 353, 249 N. W. 886.

The action for damages on affirmance of the contract can now be brought in assumpsit also under the statute permitting waiver of the tort and suit in assumpsit. C. L. 1929, § 14007, Mich. 

Stat. Ann. § 27.651. Hallett v. Gordon, 128 Mich. 364, 87 N. W. 261; Straus

Such an action (i. e., for damages) cannot be brought under the common counts but must be by a special count or declaration upon the contract. (For cases dealing with waiver of the fraud, see Monroe v. Hoffman, 276 

Mich. 281, 267 N. W. 

836; Dinius v.

The fraud relied upon must be alleged with particularity. Parker v. Armstrong, 55 Mich. 176, 20 N. W. 892; 

Pforzheimer v. Selkirk, 71 Mich. 600, 40 N. W. 12; Smith v. Thompson, 94 

Mich. 381, 54 N. W. 168; Blanksma v. 

King, 172 Mich. 666, 138 N. W. 236. 

Michigan, however, follows the minority rule as to the necessity of fraudu lent intent and holds that misrepresentations, though not intentionally fraudulent, are actionable if the one making them profits from the transaction. Holcomb v. Noble, 69 Mich. 396, 37 N. W. 

497; Aldrich v. Scribner, 154 Mich. 

23, 117 N. W. 581; Hubbard v. Oliver, 173 Mich. 337, 139 N. W. 77; Power 

Specialty Co. v. Michigan Power Co., 190 Mich. 699, 157 N. W. 408; Hillier v. Carpenter, 206 Mich. 594, 173 N. W. 

386. However an agent who has not substantially profited from the transaction cannot be held liable without fraudulent intent, Krause v. Cook, 144 

Mich. 365, 108 N. W. 81; Williamson v. Hannan, 200 Mich. 658, 166 N. W. 

829. As a general rule this exception applies to all not an actual party to the contract. Aldrich v. Scribner, supra.

It is also of course necessary to allege that the fraud was actually relied on, Brown v. Union Banking Co., 274 

Mich. 499, 265 N. W. 447; Kean v. 

Wolok, 278 Mich. 489, 270 N. W. 760; reliance upon independent investigation being fatal to the action, Urquhart v. 

Bryant, 269 Mich. 312, 257 N. W. 708.

However, under this case concerted action not amounting to a conspiracy will sustain the action, and inquiry of one so acting will not constitute independent investigation. 

Rescission and affirmance are inconsistent remedies, and when one course is chosen, constitute an election. Attorney General ex rel. Secretary of State v. State Savings & Loan Co., 290 Mich. 

212, 287 N. W. 438. The right of rescission must be exercised promptly after discovery of the fraud. Attorney

77 At common law, the rule as laid down by the Michigan Supreme Court was as follows: "1. While a landowner has the undoubted right to excavate close to the boundary line, he must take reasonable precautions to prevent his neighbor's soil from falling. "2. If he has taken such reasonable precautions, and yet the soil falls from its own pressure, he is still liable for injury to the land, but not for any injury to the superstructure. "3. If the pressure of the superstructure causes the land to fall, he is not liable either for injury to the land or superstructure. 

4. If he fails to take such reasonable precautions to protect his neighbor's soil, and to preserve it in its natural state, he is liable for the injury to both the land and superstructure, if the pressure of the superstructure did not cause the land to fall, and it fell in consequence of the failure to take such reasonable precautions. Bissell V. 

Ford, 176 Mich. 64, 141 N. W. 860.

These rules had been laid down in Gildersleeve v. Hammond, 109 Mich. 431, 67 N. W. 519, and the quoted statement is approved in Bator v. Ford Motor 

Co., 269 Mich. 648, 662, 257 N. W. 906. 

See also, Tillson v. Consumers' Power 

Co., 269 Mich. 53, 256 N. W. 801, and 

Aristos v. Detroit & Canada Tunnel Co., 258 Mich. 579, 242 N. W. 757. By statute, however, where excavation is made to a depth of "twelve feet or more below the established grade of a street, or highway upon which such land abuts or, if there be no such established grade, below the surface of the adjoining land" the owner is under an absolute obligation to furnish sufficient lateral or subjacent support to protect any buildings thereon, as well as the land. 

Act 314, P. A. 1921, C. L. 1929, § 13500, 

Mich. Stat. Ann. § 26.1141. This is an absolute obligation, and liability is not predicated upon negligence. Bator v. 

Ford Motor Co., 269 Mich. 648, 257 

N. W. 906. Such a statutory duty cannot be delegated, Bergen v. Morton 

Amusement Co., 178 App. Div. 400, 165 

N. Y. Supp. 348, and it has been held that the owner is liable even though the work was done by an independent contractor, McDaniel Bros. v. Wilson (Tex. Civ. App.), 45 S. W. (2d) 293, although it has been held that a vendor under a land contract who merely held title nominally, was not liable for breach of the duty by his vendee, Earle v. Hall, 2 Metc. (Mass.) 353. Being in derogation of the common law, such statutes are strictly construed, Tillson v. Consumers' Power Co., 269 Mich. 53, 256 

N. W. 801, but in one case at least it has been held that the owner was liable for breach of the duty when the excavation was not below the prescribed statutory depth, but the owner had intended, when the work was commenced, that it should be, Wear v. Koehler, 88 

Misc. 109, 150 N. Y. Supp. 654.

Both at common law and under the statute, the rule of damages is very broad, and covers not only actual dam- 248

80 A married woman may become personally liable for necessaries purchased and used by herself or family while living with her husband so as to charge her separate estate therefor. Campbell v. White, 22 Mich. 178; Paul v. Roberts, 50 Mich. 611, 16 N. W. 164; Hirshfield v. Waldron, 83 Mich. 116, 47 N. W.

Mich. 272, 37 N. W. 213. 

This case also holds that it must be the purchase of things which become her own separate property, being turned over to the family use as such and that she cannot bind herself to an executory agreement to support the family while living with her husband, p. 284. A note given for payment of necessaries which have been purchased on her husband's credit is voidable by the wife (though it is not void). Burge v. Pickel, 212 Mich. 398, 180 N. W. 417. If she has been deserted by her husband, she of course may also incur such liability, Carstens v. Hanselman, 61 Mich. 426, 28 N. W. 

159. The purchases will be presumed to be upon the husband's credit where she is living with him unless there is an express agreement to the contrary, Powers v. Russel, 26 Mich. 179; Burge v. 

Pickel, supra, though if they are not living together the presumption would not obtain, Pritchard v. Bigger, 288 

Mich. 447, 285 N. W. 17.

But she cannot bind herself to pay for the care of the family, Howe v.

This is of course only by statute where the title to the goods has passed to the buyer, the seller having the right to demand the return of the goods if he is still the owner by virtue of his title as in any other case of ownership and bailment. See Uniform Sales Act, § 53, C. L. 1929, § 9492, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 19.293; Waite on Sales, pp. 83-84.

The right is one possessed by the unpaid seller to reclaim possession of the goods before the buyer has acquired actual possession of them in case the buyer is found to be insolvent, whether or not the insolvency occurred subsequent to shipment. Gustine v. Phillips, 38 Mich. 674; Kingman & Co. v. Denison, 84 Mich. 608, 48 N. W. 26, 11 

L. R. A. 347, 22 Am. St. Rep. 711. See 

54 A. L. R. 184 and 31 A. L. R. 578 as to right to stop when check or draft has been dishonored. Also see Lentz v. 

Flint & P. M. Ry. Co., 53 Mich. 444, 19 

N. W. 138 on estoppel.

It has been held that the notice must inform the carrier not only of the buyer's insolvency, but that he (the seller) is unpaid, Teller & Co. v. American Ry. 

Exp. Co., 78 Pa. Super. Ct. 300; but

Glass Corp. v. New York, N. H. & H. R. 

Co., 104 Conn. 342, 133 Atl. 102, hold mere notice sufficient and under the Michigan statute no form of notice is prescribed. However, the carrier may hold up return a reasonable time for investigation. Wilson v. International 

Ry. Co., 160 N. Y. Supp. 367, aff'd 177 

App. Div. 946, 164 N. Y. Supp. 1118.

3. (Allege an accurate description of the place of the happening with any special features thereof affecting the accident including any legal characteristics, such as traffic lights, safety zone, etc.) 

4. (Allege any duties imposed upon defendant of which the court does not take judicial notice, such as duties arising from municipal ordinances.) 8 

5. (Allege that while "plaintiff was proceeding in the exercise of due care and caution" the accident occurred in such and such a manner as a proximate result of defendant's negligence, describing fully.) 4 

8"Sec. 2. Pleadings shall be as brief as the nature of the case will admit, and shall not state facts of which the courts take judicial notice, nor matters of evidence, and no pleading shall set forth any statement not required to be proved, except where specially required by rule or statute. Rule 17, Michigan

Court Rules.'' 

For this reason as well as intelligibility, the somewhat prevalent practice of alleging seriatum all of the duties imposed by law is not indicated in these forms, it being the author's belief that it is not only unnecessary but should be abandoned except as to those matters which are not the subject of judicial notice.

Municipal ordinances are not general laws and hence not judicially noticed by the courts, Motz v. Detroit, 18 

Mich. 495, but must be proven in accordance with C. L. 1929, § 14180, Mich.

Stat. Ann. § 27.875. The Michigan statutes of course are judicially noticed, C. L. 1929, § 14178, Mich. Stat. 

Ann. § 27.873; People v. River Raisin & L. E. R. Co., 12 Mich. 389, 86 Am. 

Dec. 64; Holdrige v. Farmers' & Mechanics' Bank, 16 Mich. 66; Attorney 

General Jackson v. James, 74 Mich. 733, 42 N. W. 167, and the court will consider such statutes in consideration of the pleadings on motion to dismiss. 

Little v. American State Bank of Dearborn, 263 Mich. 645, 249 N. W. 22.

This is likewise true of the statutes and common law of other states in suits involving accidents outside the state.

Walton School of Commerce v. Stroud, 

248 Mich. 84, 226 N. W. 883; Laughlin v. Michigan Motor Freight Lines, 276 

Mich. 545, 268 N. W. 887; C. L. 1929, § 14179, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 27.874. 

See Niedzinski v. Coryell, 215 Mich. 

498, 184 N. W. 476; Marples v. Standard Oil Co., 71 N. J. L. 352, 59 Atl. 32, wherein the immateriality of an allegation of duty is inferentially stated: "It is not enough for the pleader to allege that the duty exists. Such an allegation is not the statement of a fact but merely the pleader's averment of the legal efficacy of the facts which are set out in the declaration; and in considering the sufficiency of the declaration, the court does not accept the conclusion drawn by the pleader but determines for itself the legal force of those facts."' 

Seymour v. Maddox, 117 Eng. Rep. 

904, 905, 16 Q. B. 327, Lord Campbell, C. J.: "But the decisions shew that the allegation of duty is in all cases immaterial; and ought never to be introduced; for if the particular facts raise the duty, the allegation is unnecessary, and, if they do not, it will be unavailing. Also Patteson, J.: "It has been determined that it is not necessary to allege the duty where it arises from the particular facts stated in the declaration."' 

1 Chitty on Pleading 239, 16th Am. 

Ed. (1879): "The courts are also bound to take notice of all common-law rights and duties, and of general customs; and consequently these ought not to be stated in the pleading."

Schwartz v. Lindquist, 251 Ill. App. 320. It was also held in that case that such evidence was admissible under a count charging general negligence, and notwithstanding the fact that another count, charging negligence in failure to observe the lights, was withdrawn prior to the trial. 

The court said: "It is contended first that it was error to admit this evidence because there was no proof that the lights in question were installed or operated pursuant to the provisions of any ordinance or statute. The point possesses little, if any, merit. lights were there. The plaintiff said that he observed them and heeded the warning given by them. The defendant said that likewise he observed and obeyed the signals. The jurors must have known from common experience The that careful drivers of automobiles recognize lights of this kind as a device for the regulation of traffic. They must also have known that prudent drivers do not take the risk of crossing streets or boulevards with the red light against them upon the strength of the possibility that there might not be any valid ordinance requiring observance of the signals. It is finally urged that the testimony as to the lights should have been excluded because the only count in the declaration, charging the defendant with tortious conduct in failing to observe the lights, was withdrawn prior to the time of the trial. The contention is untenable. The first count of the declaration charged negligence generally. The testimony was material and competent in support of this count."' 300

1. 2. (Jurisdictional averments.) 

That on the at the City of gence, antecedent negligence, discovered negligence, discovered peril, last clear chance, intervening negligence, supervening negligence, humanitarian rule, are the same thing. Golob v. Railway, 228 Mich. 201; Gibbard v. Cursan, supra. The number and variety of such designations, two at least inaccurate, another misleading, some not generally accepted, are deplorable. If, by common consent of bench and bar, this rule, now so variously named, might be known hereafter as last clear chance, the most popular designation, many difficulties of the student, of the practitioner, and of the judge, would be removed ultimately. "If a plaintiff's negligence contributes to cause an injury, recovery is precluded. But where plaintiff's negligence is antecedent, and defendant's negligence is subsequent, it is proper to excuse plaintiff's negligence as remote, and to hold defendant's subsequently intervening negligence as proximate, in other words, to invoke the doctrine of last clear chance, and it will be noted that under this rule the defendant is guilty of negligence-nothing else, and nothing more. ""

It is thought to be essential, whenever there is a possibility that plaintiff's negligence is antecedent, to add a count under this doctrine. Otherwise plaintiff may be precluded from invoking the doctrine if the proofs subsequently warrant it. In the recent case of Cline v. Killingbeck, 288 Mich. 126, 284 N. W. 669, plaintiff, on motion for new trial, attempted to invoke the doctrine. It had not been claimed before, and was not pleaded. In affirming the denial of the trial court in permitting plaintiff to invoke the doctrine, the court quoted the opinion of the trial day of in the State of 19—, judge, saying "In this regard the court finds that such question of subsequent negligence was not pleaded, no motion was made to amend plaintiff's declaration, and nothing was mentioned in regard to after-discovered negligence until after the case had come to an end." 

And certainly one should not rely upon a declaration framed in conformity of this doctrine alone. Further language in the Cline case seems to indicate that it is essential for plaintiff to plead and prove his antecedent negligence. Thus at p. 128 it was said: "The declaration alleged due care on the part of plaintiff and negligence on the part of defendant.

The doctrine of discovered or subsequent negligence involves a confession of negligence on the part of a plaintiff and avoidance of the bar of contributory negligence by discovery or notice thereof by a defendant in time and with opportunity to prevent injury.

Inclusion of the usual allegation as to plaintiff's freedom of contributory negligence would seem, from the foregoing language, to be improper and perhaps fatal. * * * 99 Use of such a count alone, furthermore, is dangerous in that the practitioner must determine correctly that the casual connection between plaintiff's negligence and the injury is broken. Otherwise he is subjected to the usual rule that plaintiff's negligent actions continued and contributed to the injury. Harrison v. Eastern Michigan Motor Bus Co., 257 Mich. 329, 241 N. W. 131.

7. That at the time and place aforesaid have the said automobile under proper control and negligently drove live at home. Gates v. Mader, 316 Ill. 

313, 147 N. E. 241. The case was tried on the declaration and special pleas of defendant alleging that he did not operate the car by himself or agent. 

Mr. Justice Farmer said (p. 317): "If defendant had himself been driving, it could not be denied he would have been liable for negligent injury, and the decided weight of authority, we think, makes him liable, under the evidence of this case, for the negligence of the son. 

Reference is made to the cases of 

Arkin v. Page, 287 Пl. 420, 123 N. E. 

30, 5 A. L. R. 216, and Graham v. 

Page, 300 Ill. 40, 132 N. E. 817, discussed in the Gates case, in a comment in 43 Harv. L. Rev. 133. The comment is based upon the Tennessee case of 

Meinhardt v. Vaughn, 159 Tenn. 272, 17 S. W. (2d) 5, where a defendant who had bought a motorcycle and given it to his sixteen-year-old son to drive to school was held liable for injury inflicted by the boy, not on the "family purpose" theory but under principles of agency. 

See an earlier note (28 Harv. L. Rev. 

91), concluding as follows: "But it may be urged, on the other hand, that, as automobiles have latent possibilities of causing great damage, and yet are treated almost disrespectfully by the youngest children, as a matter of justice the owner should be absolutely liable for injuries inflicted. Such a rule might have a salutary effect, but its creation is within the province of the legislature, not of the courts, and should not be arrived at by distorting the principles of agency and torts to fit the case. Let not the ancient maxim be transformed to read, qui facit per auto facit per se." 

See comment, citing cases from various jurisdictions, in 65 U. S. L. Rev. 

645, and pointing out that even where the family purpose doctrine is recognized it does not depend upon the mere relationship between the person using the car and the owner thereof, but upon an agency implied from the fact that the car was purchased for family use, and the general authorization to the members of the family to employ it for such use. 

See also article in 16 A. B. 

A. Jour. 225, discussing various state statutes providing for vicarious liability.

No. 388. Action by guest passenger. 

NOTE. The "Guest Passenger Act," so called, is found in the proviso to

C. L. 1929, § 4648, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 9.1446. Its constitutionality was upheld in Naudzius v. Lahr, 253 Mich. 216, 234 N. W. 581, 30 N. C. C. A. 179, 74 A. L.

R. 1189. Plaintiff's status as a "guest" under the act is a question of fact, to be determined by the jury if in dispute, Monison v. McCoy, 266 Mich. 693, 312

FORMS No. 388 

256 N. W. 49. For a discussion of the cases as to who is a guest, see Bookhart v. Greenlease-Lied Motor Co., 215 Iowa 8, 244 N. W. 721, 82 A. L. R. 1359 and anno. at p. 1365. Also see McGuire v. Armstrong, 268 Mich. 152, 255 N. W. 

745, 36 N. C. C. A. 252; Thomas v. Currier Lumber Co., 283 Mich. 134, 277 N. W. 

857; Cardinal v. Reinecke, 280 Mich. 15, 273 N. W. 330, 274 N. W. 379; Hunter v. Baldwin, 268 Mich. 106, 255 N. W. 431. While the statute limits liability to "" gross negligence or wilful and wanton misconduct' "the term "gross negligence" has been held by the Michigan court not to mean something of less degree than wilful and wanton misconduct, Bobich v. Rogers, 258 Mich. 343, 241 

N. W. 854; Mater v. Becraft, 261 Mich. 477, 246 N. W. 191; Findlay v. Davis, 263 Mich. 179, 248 N. W. 588; Johnson v. Fremont Canning Co., 270 Mich. 524, 259 N. W. 660, and "wanton and wilful misconduct" is held to be something that differs in kind, not merely in degree, from ordinary, actionable negligence. 

Perkins v. Roberts, 272 Mich. 545, 262 N. W. 305. And a declaration, to be sufficient under this statute, must set forth more than ordinary negligence, charging defendant's action as being wanton and wilful. Naudzius v. Lahr, 253 

Mich. 216, 234 N. W. 581, 30 N. C. C. A. 179, 74 A. L. R. 1189; Michaelson v. 

Simula, 264 Mich. 457, 250 N. W. 264.

24 Where plaintiff seeks to establish wilful and wanton misconduct, the usual allegation in the declaration as to freedom from contributory negligence is unnecessary. "If a defendant be guilty of more than negligence, we pass to wilfulness or wantonness, and find ourselves entirely out of the field of negligence, for wilfulness-wantonnessrecklessness 'transcends negligence-is different in kind' (Gibbard v. Cursan, 225 Mich. 311), is 'above ordinary negligence' (Naudzius v. Lahr, 253 Mich. 216). "To a charge of wilfulness and wantonness, contributory negligence is, of course, no defense, for we are no longer in the field of negligence." 

Clark, C. J. p. 341 in Finkler v. Zimmer, 258 Mich. 336, 241 N. W. 851. 

Contributory negligence is no defense to an action based upon gross negligence or wilful or wanton misconduct.

Judgment for plaintiff was affirmed without comment on the sufficiency of the declaration. The case was decided squarely upon sections 69(1)(d) and 

69(4) being C. L. 1929, § 9508, Mich. 

Stat. Ann. § 19.309, which expressly grants a buyer the right to rescind a contract for sale after a breach of warranty, whether the contract be executory or executed. Prior to the adoption of the Uniform Sales Act in 1913, the rule was definitely laid down in Williams Transp. Line v. Darius Cole Transp. 

Co., 129 Mich. 209, 88 N. W. 473, 56 

L. R. A. 939, that in a contract of sale, the breach of a warranty of quality alone gave the buyer no right to rescind in the absence of rescission by mutual agreement, the court following the English and majority rule as laid down in 

Street v. Blay, 2 Barn. & Adol. 456.

The rule was followed in Snore v. Hammond, 140 Mich. 416, 103 N. W. 834;

Linderman Mach. Co. v. Shaw-Walker 

Co., 187 Mich. 28, 153 N. W. 34. Peculiarly, the rule was still recognized by the court following the adoption of the statute, the court in Rimmele v. 

Huebner, 190 Mich. 247, 157 N. W. 10 saying, at p. 253, "The mere breach of the warranty would not have authorized a rescission by the plaintiff alone *"' citing the Transportation case, supra. Kawecki v. Stuber-Stone Co., 218 Mich. 25, 187 N. W. 272, appears to be one of the first cases to adopt the rule as laid down in the act, and it was there done only tacitly. Parkhouse v. Hodge, 221 Mich. 308, 191 

N. W. 13, follows the Kawecki case.

For a collection of authorities on various questions involving rescission, see 

34 A. L. R. 538; 72 A. L. R. 732; 104 

A. L. R. 551. + * For rescission in equity, see Form 

No. 1087, and Youngs v. Advance- 

Rumely Thresher Co., 215 Mich. 682, 184 N. W. 535. 324

The practitioner may then be faced with the difficult problem of ascertaining what is the market price, for in many instances there may be no ready market available at the point of delivery. See 

Taylor v. Goldsmith, 228 Mich. 259, 200 

N. W. 254, which holds that the question of what constitutes a market may be a question of fact. In Balcom v. 

Tribbett, 197 Mich. 620, 164 N. W. 261, it was held that merely because there was no available market for a large stock of goods in a small town the plaintiff would not be deprived of his remedy, and in Pandaleon v. Brecker, 227 Mich. 297, 198 N. W. 953, and 

Solomon v. Richardson, 207 Mich. 415, 174 N. W. 125, it was held that when there is no available market at the point of delivery, the market price is the price at the nearest market, plus the cost of transportation. See 57 

L. R. A. 193, for annotations on "Damages for breach of contract on sale of articles that have no market price." 

41 While it is stated in 19 Encyc. Pl. & Pr. 65, that an allegation of a re-sale is not essential, the use of such an allegation is approved therein, and would seem to be proper. Seller may not only sell the goods at the place of delivery after a refusal to accept them by the buyer, but he has a duty to do so, if possible, in mitigation of damages. 

Taylor v. Goldsmith, 228 Mich. 259, 200 

N. W. 254; Pandaleon v. Brecker, 227 

Mich. 297, 198 N. W. 953; Piowaty v. 

Sheldon, 167 Mich. 218, 132 N. W. 517, Ann. Cas. 1913 A, 610. If there is no available market at the time and place of delivery, then the vendor may hold for or seek a market within a reasonable time. Piowaty v. Sheldon, Id.; 

Henry v. Hobbs, 165 Mich. 183, 130 

N. W. 616; Williams v. Robb, 104 Mich. 

242, 62 N. W. 352. A market must eventually be sought, however, either at the point of delivery, or, if necessary, elsewhere, as is indicated in the language of Pandaleon v. Brecker, supra, at p. 300: "* they were bound to sell the raisins in Detroit, the agreed point of delivery, if possible, but if impossible to there find a market plaintiffs were bound to seek a market elsewhere in order to minimize their loss." * * In connection with the right and duty of re-sale by the seller, a distinction becomes apparent, i.e. where seller seeks damages, he treats the goods in exactly the opposite manner as he does when he sues to recover the price, in the former he re-sells them as his own property to mitigate damages, in the latter he is and remains a bailee of the goods for the buyer. 329

NOTE. See C. L. 1929, § 9454, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 19.255. The above form has been taken, with modification, from Hertzler v. Manshum, 228 Mich. 416, 200 N. W. 155. This form has been simplified by eliminating the remote manufacturer as a party defendant. The manufacturer should, of course, always be named if under the circumstances there is a reasonable expectation of his liability. The two counts in the declaration predicate liability on a theory of breach of implied warranty and of negligence, as was done in the Hertzler case. 

The joinder of these two counts was impliedly approved by the court in its opinion, which, however, in one way confused the question as to upon which theory recovery might be had, particularly as to the retailer, by saying, at p. 423: "The implied warranty, so-called, reaching from the manufacturer of food stuffs to the ultimate purchaser for immediate consumption is in the nature of a representation that the highest degree of care has been exercised and a breach of such duty inflicting personal injury is a wrong in the nature of a tort and not a mere breach of contract to be counted on in assumpsit. Except in name and to establish privity between the manufacturer and the ultimate consumer it is the same thing as negligence. Plaintiff's case, in its last analysis, is bottomed on negligence. But see Cheli v. Cudahy Bros. Co., 267 Mich. 690, 255 N. W. 414, wherein the Hertzler case was cited as authority for the propriety of joining both a count for breach of warranty and one for negligence, and wherein the liability of a manufacturer of food on implied warranty only seems to have been denied because the food was consumed in an unusual way, although no negligence was found to exist on the part of the manufacturer. 

In this class of case the court seems to adopt a doctrine closely approximating 334

FORMS 

No. 407 the rule of res ipsa loquitur. As was pointed out in Hertzler v. Manshum, supra, plaintiff had the burden to prove that the flour contained poison. Once this fact was established, however, then the plaintiff had made a prima facie case, and the burden was on defendants to excuse themselves.

74 The use of a rule nisi raises the question of whether such a rule, after the expiration of the time limit, becomes a final order in the sense that it may be appealed from. No case on the point was found in Michigan, but the United States Supreme Court, in Alley v. Nott, 111 U. S. 472, 28 L. Ed. 491, 4 Sup. Ct. 495, held that an order sus- 

Circuit Judge. taining a demurrer is a final order, unless leave to plead over or the right of amendment is given. Consequently, if a rule nisi is entered, the only safe practice following the expiration of the time limit without amendment would be to enter final judgment reciting such fact. 14 365

The author does not think this inconsistent with the statutory permission to raise such issue by answer and have it heard in advance of trial upon notice by either party. The statute reads as follows: "Demurrer, pleas in abatement, and pleas to the juris-. diction, are abolished. All questions heretofore raised by such plea or demurrer, shall hereafter be raised by motion to dismiss, or in the answer or notice attached to the plea; and in case such questions are raised by answer, or by notice attached to the plea, the same may be brought up for determination by the court, in advance of the trial of the cause, upon four (4) days' notice by either party. The plaintiff shall at any time, either before or after the hearing of the questions so 

Attorney for Defendant.75 raised, be entitled to amend his pleadings, so as to meet the objections raised thereto, upon such terms as the court may deem proper." C. L. 1929, § 14120, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 27.814.

89Sec. 1. The general issue is abolished, and answers shall be used wherever pleas have been employed in actions at law.

The common counts in assumpsit not being abolished, a general denial of the common counts shall be sufficient. "Sec. 2. Every answer shall contain an explicit admission or denial of each allegation in the declaration or bill of complaint as to which the defendant has knowledge or belief. But as to matters charged in the declaration or bill as to which the defendant avers he has no knowledge sufficient to form a belief, he shall not be required to admit or deny the same, but shall state his want of such knowledge. 

And every material allegation in the declaration or bill to which the defendant shall not make answer shall be taken as admitted by the defendant. In connection with every denial, the answer shall set forth the substance of the matters which will be relied upon to support such denial. 

When an unverified bill of particulars is filed with any of the common counts, the answer shall deal with the items therein set forth in the same manner as though they were alleged in the declaration." Michigan Court Rule 23, 88 1, 2. 379

95"No doubt it is the rule, and one recently applied in decisions of this court, that fraud in the procurement of insurance is provable as a defense in an action at law upon the policy, resort to equity being unnecessary to render that defense available." Cardozo, J. in 

American Life Ins. Co. v. Stewart, 300 

U. S. 203, 81 L. Ed. 605, 57 Sup. Ct. 377. 

As to materiality as a matter of law of misrepresentation in application for insurance policy, see comment, based on 

Geer v. Union Mut. Life Ins. Co., 273 

N. Y. 261, 7 N. E. (2d) 125, in 7 Brooklyn L. Rev. 252.

In the law of insurance a misrepre sentation by the insured is an oral or written statement of a material fact or condition affecting the risk, made by the insured to the insurer, which precedes and is not a part of the contract, unless it expressly stipulated that it shall be, and is either intentionally untrue or made with a reckless disregard for its truth or falsity. Zolintakis v. 

Equitable Life Assur. Soc. of United 

States (C. C. A. 10th, 1938), 97 F. (2d) 583. "The statements made by the insured in the application are by the terms of the policy specifically made representations and not warranties. Consequently, the defendant to be entitled to judgment must establish that the insured's statements were materially false and that insured knew this at the time he made them." Johnson, J., in Clum v.

Guardian Life Ins. Co. (D. C. Pa. 

1938), 24 F. Supp. 396. 

A material fact is any fact, the knowledge or ignorance of which would naturally influence the insurer's judgment in making the contract, in estimating the degree and character of the risk or in fixing the rate of insurance. 

Zolintakis v. Equitable Life Assur. Soc. of United States (C. C. A. 10th, 1938), 97 F. (2d) 583.

The exercise of the utmost good faith is required of parties about to enter into an insurance contract, and the suppression of the material facts which a party is bound in good faith to disclose 384

1 See, "Courts have frequently used accord and satisfaction as a single expression. The failure to differentiate between the two has, as a result, proven confusing. Not only have these words been used interchangeably, but various other terms, such as 'compromise and settlement,' 'novation,' and 'substituted agreement' have been used in stead. Separate definitions of accord and satisfaction, respectively, will necessarily clarify the legal issues involved. 

It is generally agreed that an accord is ordinarily a bilateral contract in which one party agrees to accept, in the future, in satisfaction of a liquidated or disputed claim arising out of a tort or contract, a stipulated performance which the other party agrees to tender. Satisfaction is the actual and full performance of this agreement.'' 

Note in 7 Brooklyn Law Rev. 97. 394

5Estoppel in equity must rest on substantial grounds of prejudice or change of position, not on technicalities.'' 

Hughes, C. J., in Ashwander v.

Tennessee Valley Authority, 297 U. S. 

288, 80 L. Ed. 688, 56 Sup. Ct. 588. 

To constitute estoppel (1) there must be false representation or wrongful misleading silence; (2) the error must originate in a statement of fact and not in an opinion or a statement of law; (3) the person claiming the benefits of estoppel must be ignorant of the true facts, and (4) be adversely affected by the acts or statements of the person against whom an estoppel is claimed. 

Van Antwerp v. United States (C. C.

6The courts should be diligent in searching and weeding out hidden illegal exactions in contracts of lenders of money. Hamilton, J., in In re

An agreement that the money advanced is to be repaid absolutely and unconditionally is an essential element of a usurious contract. Sachs v. Ginsberg (C. C. A. 5th, 1936), 87 F. (2d) 28. "Usury imports the existence of four elements: (1) A loan or forbearance, either express or implied; (2) an understanding between the parties that the principal shall be repaid absolutely; (3) the exaction of a greater profit than allowed by law; and (4) an intention to violate the law. The last may be implied if the first three are present. Hamilton, J., in Jenkins v. 

Dugger (C. C. A. 6th, 1938), 96 F. (2d) 727.

This time runs from the last item in the case of open accounts, and in the case of infants and persons under disability does not run until its removal.

11 This form may be adapted to the case of an assault against a child, mother, servant or master.

The answer corresponding to the former plea of son assault demesne is used where it is sought to justify what would amount to a trespass by showing that the plaintiff was in fact the aggressor and defendant acted in defense of his rights. 

No recovery may be had for an assault and battery to prevent or abate a trespass if no more force be used than is reasonably necessary. What is reasonably necessary is a question of fact. 

Escandon v. Pan American Foreign 

Corp. (C. C. A. 5th, 1937), 88 F. (2d) 

276, aff'g (D. C. Tex. 1935), 12 F.

Supp. 1006. 

Under answer in the nature of plea of son assault demesne, a wounding may be authorized in self-defense; but where the law prima facie only authorizes an arrest, or touching a person, if a wounding is attempted to be justified the rule has been that the occasion thereof must be specially alleged. In defense of the person, an assault and battery may be justified, but in defense of the possession of property, defendant must make answer in the nature of molliter manus imposuit. See discussion in

Puterbaugh on Common Law Pleading and Practice, § 340, and authorities there cited.

By answer in the nature of the former plea of son assault demesne in an action for assault and battery the defendant assumes the burden of proving not only that the plaintiff first assaulted him and that he, the defendant, acted in necessary self-defense, but also that in defending himself he used no more force than was necessary. See Hale v. 

Harms, 257 Ill. App. 388.

By plea of son assault demesne, defendant assumes the burden of proving not only that plaintiff first assaulted him and that he, the defendant, acted only in necessary self-defense, but that in so defending himself he used no more force than was necessary. Gizler v. 

Witzel, 82 Ill. 322; Spenler v. Turley, 158 Ill. App. 146; Reimenschneider v. 

Neusis, 175 Ill. App. 172.

In trespass for simple assault, answer in the nature of plea of molliter manus imposuit, in reasonable efforts to prevent a breach of the peace by plaintiff's assault on a third person, is good, but otherwise when the declaration alleges aggravated force on the part of defendant. The general principle has been that such plea is not a full answer to a complaint charging assault and wounding and that in such case there must be either a denial of the beating, wounding, etc., or a statement of facts and circumstances by way of justification. See discussion in

Puterbaugh on Common Law Pleading and Practice, § 343, and authorities there cited.

In the absence of a plea of molliter manus imposuit, proof that the assault and battery in question took place in an effort to preserve the peace is inadmissible as a substantive ground of defense, but is competent, notwithstanding the absence of such plea, in diminution of damages. Merrifield v. Davis, 130 Ill. 

App. 162.

No. 554. Res judicata-General form of defense of.14 

That on the

AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE. 

day of plaintiff brought an action in the 14The rule of res judicata is based upon that public policy which requires that a single controversy which is capa ble of being completely determined in one suit shall be ended by the judg ment in that suit and shall not become the subject matter of subsequent litigation." Sanborn, J., in Guettel v. 

United States (C. C. A. 8th, 1938), 95 

F. (2d) 229, aff'g (D. C. Mo. 1936), 17 F. Supp. 725. 

A plea of res judicata barring a second suit cannot be sustained unless predicated upon a final judgment determining the rights of the parties. 

National Liberty Ins. Co. of America v. Police Jury of Natchitoches Parish 

(C. C. A. 5th, 1938), 96 F. (2d) 261. 

Any right, fact, or matter, in issue and directly adjudicated, or necessarily involved in the determination of an action before a competent court in which a judgment or decree has been rendered upon its merits, is conclusively settled by the judgment therein and cannot again be litigated between the same parties and their privies, whether the claim, demand, purpose, or subject matter is the same or not. Beck v. Hill (C. C. A. 10th, 1937), 91 F. (2d) 75. "For the purpose of making the 19—, court of prior judgment conclusive, it is not essential that the parties be actually identical in both causes, provided a party in one suit is in privity with the corresponding party in the other suit." 

Coleman, J., in Western Maryland Ry.

Co. v. U. S. (D. C. Md. 1938), 23 F. 

Supp. 554.

As to effect of a former judgment in a subsequent suit between codefendants see comment, based on Central 

Surety & Ins. Co. v. Mississippi Export 

R. R. Co. (C. C. A. 5th, 1937), in 10 

Miss. L. Jour. 319. 

As to conclusiveness of judgment on merits in favor of a servant in action against the master, see comment, based on Good Health Dairy Products Corp. v. Emery, 275 N. Y. 14, 9 N. E. (2d) 

758, in 7 Brooklyn L. Rev. 113. 

See comment, "Res Judicata-Suits for Services-Effect of Prior Adjudi cation on Subsequent Action for Unlawful Discharge," based on Larme 

Estates v. Omnichrome Corp., 275 N. Y. 

426, 10 N. E. (2d) 793. 

See article, "Res Judicata and Collateral Attack," by Jay Leo Rothschild, 7 Brooklyn L. Rev. 271.

C. L. 1929, § 14139, Mich. Stat. Ann. § 27.833. And by statute notice of recoupment was required to be annexed to the plea of the general issue, with a

NOTE. The remedy and procedure with reference to summary judgments is provided in C. L. 1929, §§ 14260, 14261, Mich. Stat. Ann. §§ 27.989, 27.990, and 455

No. 606

Rule 30, Michigan Court Rules. Also see text, Vol. 1, Chap. XXXVI, p.

459, for a general discussion.

A distinction should be drawn between motions for judgment on the pleadings and motions for summary judgment, the two having sometimes been confused in practice. In the former, judgment is sought because, as the pleadings stand, there is no question of fact to be determined, and the case may be disposed of on the law and its merits at that point. In the latter, an issue has been raised by a pleading which in fact may not exist, and the court determines its existence from the affidavits and record on the motion.

I. INTERVENTION. 

NOTE. Care should be used to determine whether the relief can be obtained by intervention or whether an ancillary or independent bill should be employed, intervention if used in an improper manner being a bar to questioning the very action sought to be questioned. Livingston v. Southern Surety Co. of New York, 262 Mich. 438, 247 N. W. 712. (See note 43, infra.) 

No. 609. Petition for leave to intervene.

Petitioner therefore prays that on the hearing of this petition he may be granted the following relief: (a) That an order may be made granting leave to petitioner to intervene in said cause upon such terms as shall be prescribed by the court (for the purpose of -). 458

No. 610 (b) That petitioner may have such other and such further relief as the nature of his case may require.

No. 610. Order. 

(Caption.) 

In the above entitled cause the motion (or petition) of for leave to intervene as a defendant in said cause having been regularly brought on to be heard and after hearing 

43 Consult text, Vol. 3, Chap. 

LXXXVII, p. 354. 

Intervention must be in recognition of the propriety of the main proceeding and in subordination thereto, except in the case of one claiming to own property which has been attached may intervene for the purpose of moving to release the attachment upon such property. C. L. 1929, § 14019, Mich. Stat. 

Ann. § 27.663. And while it has been held that one who intervenes and is made a party defendant can defend the case and defeat recovery, Weatherby v. 

Kent Circuit Judge, 194 Mich. 46, 160 

N. W. 611, still he must accept the pleadings as he finds them, Weatherby v. Kent Circuit Judge, supra, and there may be no objection to the jurisdiction of the court, no attempt to set aside its appointment of a receiver, etc., or any motion to dismiss, but such relief if sought must be by an ancillary bill in equity. Michigan Trust Co. v. National 

Bank of Ionia, 241 Mich. 146, 216 N. W. 

472; Livingston v. Southern Surety Co. of New York, 262 Mich. 438, 247 N. W. 

712. (The only exception, of course, is the right of the attorney general, intervening under C. L. 1929, § 187, Mich. 

Stat. Ann. § 3.211, as a matter of right and at any stage of the proceedings, to move to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction or take any other steps that might be taken by one of the parties, Russell v. 

People's Wayne County Bank of Highland Park, 275 Mich. 415, 266 N. W. 

401.) It has also been held that an intervening plaintiff in a mandamus proceeding to compel the payment of bonds can share in the fund only after the plaintiff has received payment and has no right to pro-rate with the original plaintiff. John Wittbold & Co. v. 

City of Ferndale, 281 Mich. 503, 275 N.

W. 225. It has also been held that where a proper plaintiff intervenes in a suit by an improper plaintiff, the court will not go through the idle ceremony of dismissing the suit on defendant's motion and compelling the intervening plaintiff to bring a new action. King v. Emmons, 283 Mich. 116, 277 N. W. 851, 115 A. L. R. 564. (For procedure on an ancillary bill attacking the propriety of the main proceeding, consult Michigan Trust Co. v. National Bank of Ionia, 241 Mich. 

146, 216 N. W. 472.) 

The statute providing for intervention applies both at law and in equity. 459

53 See C. L. 1929, §§ 14160-14167,

54 See text, Vol. 3, § 1366, p. 367. 

An affidavit setting forth the reasons for taking the depositions is not necessary, the setting forth of such reasons in the notice being sufficient. Patterson v. Wabash, St. L. & P. Ry., 54 

Mich. 91, 19 N. W. 761; Colton v. 

Rupert, 60 Mich. 318, 27 N. W. 520; 

Wanner v. Wayne Circuit Judge, 169 

Mich. 231, 134 N. W. 993. "Before any depositions so taken can be read in evidence at the trial of the cause, it must be made to appear satisfactorily to the judge that the reason stated in the notice for taking the testimony existed at the time it was taken. An undisputed affidavit to that effect would establish it prima facie; but, where contradicted under oath, the court must pass upon the issue, and the reasons for taking the depositions must be shown as a matter of fact to have existed at the time, before they can be used at the trial.'' Wanner v. Wayne 

Circuit Judge, supra. 476

65Sec. 1. Application may be made by petition to any court of record in term time, or to the judge thereof in vacation, to compel the production and discovery of books, papers and documents relating to the merits of any action or suit pending in such court, or of any defense to such action or suit, in the following cases: (a) By the plaintiff, to compel the discovery of papers or documents in the possession of or under the control of the defendant, which may be necessary to enable the plaintiff to declare or answer to any pleading of the defendant. (b) The plaintiff may be compelled to make the discovery of papers or documents, where the same shall be necessary to enable the defendant to answer any pleading of the plaintiff. (c) The plaintiff may be compelled, after declaring, and the defendant, after pleading, to produce and discover all papers or documents on which the action or defense is founded. (d) After issue joined in any action, either party may be compelled to produce and discover all such books, papers and documents, as may be necessary to enable the party applying for such discovery to prepare for the trial of the cause. 'Sec. 2. The petition for such discovery shall state the facts and circumstances on which the same is claimed, and shall be verified by affidavit, stating that the books, papers and documents whereof discovery is sought are not in the possession or under the control of the party applying therefor, and that the party making such affidavit is advised by his counsel and verily believes, that the discovery of the books, papers or documents, mentioned in such petition, is necessary to enable him to declare, or answer, or to prepare for trial, as the case may be. Notice of the hearing of such petition shall be given as provided in Rules 8, 9 and 10."

Michigan Court Rule 40, §§ 1, 2.

66''Sec. 3. The rule granting the discovery shall specify the mode in which the same is to be made, which may be either by requiring the party to deliver sworn copies of matters to be discovered, or by requiring him to produce and deposit the same with the clerk of the court in which the trial is to be had. The order shall also specify the time within which the discovery should be made. "Sec. 4. The court, or presiding judge thereof, in granting such order, shall be governed by the principles and practice of the court of chancery in compelling discovery, except that the costs of such proceedings shall always be awarded in the discretion of the court. "Sec. 5. Every such order may be vacated by the court, or the judge granting the same: (a) Upon satisfactory evidence that it should not have been granted. (b) Upon the discovery sought being obtained. (c) Upon the party required to make discovery denying on oath the possession or control of the books, papers or documents ordered so to be produced. 'Sec. 6. When an order directing the discovery of books, papers or documents, has been made, the court may, in its discretion and on terms, order a stay of proceedings, until such order for discovery shall have been complied with or vacated; and the party obtaining such order, after the same shall have been complied with or vacated, shall have the like time to declare, plead or answer, to which he was entitled at the time of making the order."

Michigan Court Rule 40, §§ 3-6.
